plot: Odo and Mothwick follow the true story of Shackleton's crossing of South Georgia (May 1916): after the Endurance is lost, Shackleton, Worsley and Crean cross unmapped mountains for 36 hours to save 22 men on Elephant Island, and Shackleton feels they were 'four, not three'; the twist is that all three secretly felt the extra companion and only admitted it weeks later — today called the Third Man factor — and the story ends with every man rescued.

beats.say: 1916, South Georgia. Three men crossed the ice, but felt four.
Four? There were only three of them. So who was the fourth?
A true story, written by Ernest Shackleton in his own book.
Three frozen men, Odo. Remember that number. Three.
Their ship, Endurance, was crushed by Antarctic sea ice in 1915.
Twenty-eight men were left with nothing but the frozen sea.
They drifted for months, then rowed to Elephant Island.
Nobody will ever look for us here. So we go to them.
Six men sailed a tiny open boat eight hundred miles.
After about two weeks, they reached South Georgia. On the wrong side.
The whaling station was beyond mountains and glaciers no one had crossed.
May nineteenth, three in the morning. Shackleton, Worsley and Crean set off.
Screws from the boat, Boss. In our boots, for grip.
No tent. No sleeping bags. Just rope, a stove, and an adze.
If they fail, Odo, twenty-two men on that island are lost.
High on a ridge, night fell fast. Fog climbed up behind them.
We can't stay up here. We'll freeze. We slide.
They coiled the rope, sat on it, and slid into the dark.
At one stop, Shackleton let the other two sleep for five minutes.
Up, both of you. You've slept half an hour. Let's go.
That night, Shackleton felt something he could not explain.
Later, he wrote it down in his book, South.
It seemed to me often that we were four, not three.
Four. But we counted three, Odo. Only three.
New true story every day. Subscribe so you never miss one.
Dawn. At about half past six, a faint sound rose from below.
A steam whistle. The whalers, called to work. People!
The first sound from the outside world in seventeen months.
May twentieth, afternoon. Three ragged men walked into Stromness.
Who are you three? I don't know you.
My name is Shackleton.
They made it, Odo. But who walked beside them out there?
Here is the strangest part. On the march, Shackleton said nothing.
Weeks later, Worsley was the first to speak.
Boss, on that march I kept feeling another person with us.
So did I. The whole way across.
All three felt it... and each kept it a secret?
In 1933, the climber Frank Smythe was alone high on Everest.
Here. Take half of my mint cake.
He turned to hand it over. Nobody was there.
Today it has a name: the Third Man factor.
Doctors think a mind at its limit can give itself a companion.
A poet read Shackleton's book and wrote it into The Waste Land.
Who is the third who walks always beside you?
And the twenty-two men on Elephant Island? Every one came home.
Maybe it doesn't matter who it was. It got them home.
Liked this? The Baychimo ghost ship story is next on the channel.
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.

long.title: Snow 1916: Who Walked With Shackleton? | True Story Animated
long.description:
Previous true story: https://youtu.be/ZjsuX8aDNa0

"Three men crossed the mountains. All three felt a fourth." — Odo

A true story from South Georgia, May 1916: after the Endurance was crushed by the ice, Ernest Shackleton, Frank Worsley and Tom Crean crossed unmapped mountains for 36 hours to save their 22 stranded men. Shackleton later wrote that it often seemed they were four, not three.
